item.title: FMA defends unnecessary road noise claim in bike show
item.description: The Fiji Motorcyclists Association says a recent motorcycle convoy was part of an organised and controlled Bike Show entry, while stressing that it does not condone unnecessary noise or disruptive behaviour on public roads. According to the association, its members had been officially invited to participate in the event and Police approval had been provided.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Motorcyclists Association says a recent motorcycle convoy was part of an organised and controlled Bike Show entry, while stressing that it does not condone unnecessary noise or disruptive behaviour on public roads.

According to the association, its members had been officially invited to participate in the event and Police approval had been provided.

“The motorcycle entry was part of an organised and controlled environment, where members were participating in the Bike Show and creating awareness of motorcycles and the motorcycling community,” the FMA said.

The association acknowledged concerns raised about noise but said it was not aware of any formal complaint being lodged with either the FMA or event organisers over the particular incident.

“We are aware of comments regarding noise being generated. However, to our knowledge, no official complaint has been made or lodged with the FMA or the event organisers regarding this particular incident.”

The FMA stressed that its support for motorcycle events should not be interpreted as endorsing excessive road noise.

“FMA wishes to make its position clear that we do not condone unnecessary noise pollution, excessive revving, reckless riding or disruptive behaviour on public roads by any of our members.”

However, the association said the circumstances of the event also needed to be considered, noting that performance motorcycles naturally produce significant engine sound.

It said controlled displays were part of showcasing motorcycles and raising public awareness of their presence on Fiji’s roads.

“Being seen and heard can also contribute to motorcycle safety by reminding other road users to be aware of motorcycles and share the road responsibly,” the FMA said.

The association says it remains committed to promoting safe, responsible and respectful motorcycling while working with the Fiji Police Force, relevant authorities, event organisers and the wider community.

item.title: Heavy rain alert remains in force for parts of Fiji
item.description: A heavy rain alert remains in force for Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands as a trough of low pressure affects the western part of the country. The National Weather Forecasting Centre in Nadi says occasional rain, isolated heavy falls and thunderstorms are expected over the affected areas today.
item.content:encoded:
A heavy rain alert remains in force for Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands as a trough of low pressure affects the western part of the country.

The National Weather Forecasting Centre in Nadi says occasional rain, isolated heavy falls and thunderstorms are expected over the affected areas today.

The alert was maintained in the 5.30am weather bulletin issued this morning.

An easterly wind flow currently prevails over Fiji, while a trough of low pressure continues to affect western parts of the country.

Cloudy periods with some showers are forecast for other parts of Fiji.

Moderate to fresh easterly winds are expected, with moderate to rough seas.

Wet conditions are forecast to continue into Monday.

The outlook is for occasional rain, isolated heavy falls and thunderstorms to persist over Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands.

Cloudy periods with some showers are expected elsewhere.

The heavy rain alert remains in effect for the identified areas as the trough continues to influence conditions over the country.

item.title: Parliament to debate $200M Fiji Airways Government loan guarantee
item.description: Parliament will on Monday debate a motion seeking approval for the Government to guarantee an additional $200 million in borrowings by Fiji Airways. According to the parliamentary schedule of motions for debate, the Minister for Finance will move the motion under section 145(1) of the Constitution and Standing Order 131.
item.content:encoded:
Parliament will on Monday debate a motion seeking approval for the Government to guarantee an additional $200 million in borrowings by Fiji Airways.

According to the parliamentary schedule of motions for debate, the Minister for Finance will move the motion under section 145(1) of the Constitution and Standing Order 131.

The motion seeks Parliament’s approval for the Government to guarantee Fiji Airways’ additional borrowings of $200 million for three years, effective from August 1, 2026 to June 30, 2029.

It also proposes that Fiji Airways be exempted from paying a guarantee fee to the Government.

The motion further seeks approval for the Government guarantees covering the specified borrowing facilities to remain in place until the facilities reach full maturity or are discharged.

The proposed guarantee comes several years after Parliament was asked to approve increases to government-backed borrowing for the national airline following the severe impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on international aviation.

In October 2021, Parliament considered a proposal to increase the existing local borrowing guarantee for Fiji Airways from $191.1 million to $241.1 million.

The proposed offshore borrowing guarantee was also increased from US$117.1 million to US$142.1 million.

At the time, the changes took the total government guarantee ceiling for Fiji Airways from approximately FJ$455 million to FJ$561.4 million.

The 2021 proposal also provided for Fiji Airways to be exempt from paying a guarantee fee and for the guarantees to remain valid until the relevant borrowing facilities were discharged or fully settled.

Monday’s motion will put the national carrier’s government-backed borrowing arrangements back before Parliament, with MPs being asked to approve the additional $200 million guarantee and associated conditions.

item.title: Ministry puts parties on notice
item.description: PRIOR approval must be given by the Ministry of Education before any school facility is used for political party campaigns. Minister for Education Aseri Radrodro said this approval must be given by the ministry’s permanent secretary Navin Raj.
item.content:encoded:
PRIOR approval must be given by the Ministry of Education before any school facility is used for political party campaigns.

Minister for Education Aseri Radrodro said this approval must be given by the ministry’s permanent secretary Navin Raj.

“According to MOE Policy, any use of the school should have the prior approval of PSE,” Mr Radrodro said.

“The request should have clearly stipulated the purpose of the request for use of schools and the logistics involved.”

Mr Radrodro raised concerns about the recent use of a Nadi school facility by a new political party last month.

“In this instance I can state that the head of school in the subject school has not requested for any approval for the use of the school for political gathering.”

Section 113 of the Electoral Act 2014 state it is unlawful to conduct campaign activities or to post or distribute any campaign material inside a public office or infrastructure including schools.

Subsection 4 bans the use of any government-owned vehicle to conduct campaign activities unless the vehicle is being explicitly deployed to provide required security.

item.title: National ID will ensure help reaches those in need, says Kamikamica
item.description: THE proposed national identification system will help Government better target welfare, education assistance and other public services while reducing the potential for people to access support they do not need. Speaking to The Fiji Times online portal The Lens@177, Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica said the national ID will allow Government to accurately identify individuals receiving grants
item.content:encoded:
THE proposed national identification system will help Government better target welfare, education assistance and other public services while reducing the potential for people to access support they do not need.

Speaking to The Fiji Times online portal The Lens@177, Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica said the national ID will allow Government to accurately identify individuals receiving grants and allowances, helping ensure assistance reaches those who genuinely need it.

“With a national ID, we can actually zero in and identify people that really need the assistance,” he said.

He believes the system could also deliver savings by identifying households that are financially capable of meeting some costs themselves.

Mr Kamikamica pointed to free school fees and back-to-school allowances, saying some well-off families have told him they would be willing to pay rather than receive Government assistance.

Cabinet has endorsed the draft National Identification Bill 2026 which is intended to establish a secure national identity framework to improve access to Government and private-sector services, strengthen digital governance, support financial inclusion and improve service delivery.

The program has been developed following stakeholder and public consultations, with technical support from the Asian Development Bank. The proposed legislation includes safeguards covering privacy, data protection and the secure handling of personal and biometric information.

Following passage of the legislation, implementation is expected to move through system development, pilot testing and nationwide registration.

item.title: Man banned from drinking alcohol in Tavua for 15 months
item.description: A man has been prohibited from drinking alcohol in prohibited places within the Tavua Town boundary for the next 15 months. Resident Magistrate Timoci Qalinauci imposed the order on Setareki Naeqe at the Tavua Magistrates’ Court on August 10 after convicting him of drinking liquor in a prohibited place and disobedience of a lawful order.
item.content:encoded:
A man has been prohibited from drinking alcohol in prohibited places within the Tavua Town boundary for the next 15 months.

Resident Magistrate Timoci Qalinauci imposed the order on Setareki Naeqe at the Tavua Magistrates’ Court on August 10 after convicting him of drinking liquor in a prohibited place and disobedience of a lawful order.

According to the agreed facts, the Tavua Magistrates’ Court had previously ordered Naeqe on October 27, 2025, not to drink alcohol in Tavua Town for 12 months.

However, on August 7 this year, police officers conducting a beat patrol saw Naeqe standing on a footpath beside the Tavualevu public toilet drinking a glass of rum and cola.

The court heard that when police approached him, Naeqe ran towards the village before being chased and arrested.

Magistrate Qalinauci said Naeqe had disregarded the earlier court order.

“The court denounces your offending for the disregard of the court order,” he said.

The magistrate also noted that Naeqe had previous convictions, including two previous cases of drinking liquor in a prohibited place.

“You are a recidivist of similar offence of Count 1,” Magistrate Qalinauci said.

Naeqe was sentenced to two months imprisonment for drinking liquor in a prohibited place and four months for disobedience of a lawful order. The sentences will run concurrently, giving him an effective four-month prison term.

In addition, Magistrate Qalinauci imposed a new 15-month restriction.

The court ordered Naeqe “not to drink liquor, wine or spirit in a prohibited place” within the Tavua Town boundary for the next 15 months.

The magistrate warned that breaching the order could result in Naeqe being charged again with disobedience of a lawful order under the Crimes Act 2009.

Naeqe has 28 days to appeal to the High Court.

item.title: High Court criticises ‘evil people’s designs’ comment
item.description: The High Court has criticised comments made by Commission of Inquiry Commissioner Justice David Ashton-Lewis about former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali, finding they were inappropriate and could be viewed as demonstrating apparent bias against her. Justice Dane Tuiqereqere highlighted the remarks in his judgment quashing the COI findings and declaring the report null and void.
item.content:encoded:
The High Court has criticised comments made by Commission of Inquiry Commissioner Justice David Ashton-Lewis about former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali, finding they were inappropriate and could be viewed as demonstrating apparent bias against her.

Justice Dane Tuiqereqere highlighted the remarks in his judgment quashing the COI findings and declaring the report null and void.

The comments were made by Justice Ashton-Lewis during a radio interview on May 29, 2025, after the COI report had been completed but before it was released publicly.

Justice Tuiqereqere said remarks made about Malimali during the interview “were not appropriate and may be construed, by a fair-minded fully informed observer, as an apparent bias against Ms Malimali”.

During the interview, Justice Ashton-Lewis made a series of strongly worded claims about Malimali, including that she had been “universally seen as corrupt” and as someone who would protect high-ranking people.

He also questioned why Malimali had been so important to those who wanted her appointed.

“Now the question then arises why was she so important?” Justice Ashton-Lewis said during the interview.

“Well, the rest of the evidence shows she was so important because she would do evil people’s designs…”

Justice Tuiqereqere highlighted the comments while considering whether the Commissioner’s conduct met the legal test for apparent bias.

Justice Ashton-Lewis had also said during the interview that Malimali was “unsuitable for the job” and “unqualified for the job by dint of her background”, and claimed that “no one trusts her”.

The High Court did not find sufficient evidence to establish actual bias by the Commissioner.

However, Justice Tuiqereqere found that the test for apparent bias was clearly satisfied when the Commissioner’s conduct, the COI report and his subsequent statements were considered.

The court’s distinction means it did not conclude Justice Ashton-Lewis was personally or actually biased, but found the circumstances were sufficient for a fair-minded and fully informed observer to reasonably apprehend a lack of impartiality.

The apparent bias finding was among the significant problems identified by the High Court with the conduct of the inquiry and its report.

item.title: Government says foundations laid for diversified economy
item.description: THE Coalition Government has laid important foundations for a more diversified Fijian economy, despite scepticism from some members of the public over whether enough has been achieved during its term. Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica says Government’s focus has increasingly shifted towards developing industries beyond Fiji’s traditional economic pillars, with commercial agriculture, ICT, tou
item.content:encoded:
THE Coalition Government has laid important foundations for a more diversified Fijian economy, despite scepticism from some members of the public over whether enough has been achieved during its term.

Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica says Government’s focus has increasingly shifted towards developing industries beyond Fiji’s traditional economic pillars, with commercial agriculture, ICT, tourism, coffee, mahogany and kava identified as areas with significant potential.

He says Fiji Water’s investment in a citrus farm in Labasa and interest from Sri Lanka-based Aitken Spence in commercial agriculture demonstrate growing private-sector confidence.

In the technology sector, Mr Kamikamica points to Google’s investment in Fiji, the introduction of Starlink and the deployment of 5G, saying these developments will expand connectivity and create new economic opportunities.

Tourism investment, he says, is another indication of the country’s potential. Mr Kamikamica said about $2billion in construction is currently underway, including four major hotel projects being developed concurrently.

He also highlights specialty coffee, saying a 120-acre farm in Rakiraki could help establish a high-value coffee industry. According to Mr Kamikamica, investors believe the sector could potentially generate $50million within 10 years if properly managed.

Mahogany, which he says has the potential to become a $100million industry, is also undergoing reforms, while a proposed kava bill is expected to improve quality control and unlock greater export opportunities.

Mr Kamikamica acknowledges that many Fijians remain unconvinced by the Government’s record, but argues that much of its work involves addressing long-standing problems.

He points to improvements in water infrastructure, roads and the health system, including efforts to address challenges at CWM Hospital.

Asked whether the coalition will secure another term, Mr Kamikamica said the decision rests with voters.

“That’s the beauty of democracy. At the end of the day, it’s the people of Fiji that see what’s happening.”

He said the Government’s priority was to continue delivering and better communicate its achievements to the public.
